paragraphs.heading: A lord's fortified home
paragraphs.text: A castle was a fortified building of the Middle Ages, put up mostly by nobles, royalty and military orders. Scholars define it as a private fortified residence: the home of a lord that was also a stronghold. That sets it apart from a palace or villa, which existed mainly for pleasure, and from older shared defences such as Anglo-Saxon burhs or walled cities like Constantinople. Local feudal lords built and owned castles, whether for their own use or on behalf of their monarch.

paragraphs.heading: Why castles appeared
paragraphs.text: European castles first went up in the 9th and 10th centuries, after the Carolingian Empire fell and its land was split among lords and princes. Each noble built one to control the ground around it. A castle worked both ways in war: it was a base for launching raids and a shelter from enemies. It was also a seat of government and a sign of power. Town castles watched over local people and key roads, while country castles often sat near mills, good farmland or water.

paragraphs.heading: Holding a conquered land
paragraphs.text: The Norman conquest of England shows a castle being used to attack as well as defend. Norman invaders built castles to protect themselves and to keep the English population under control. As William the Conqueror pushed across the country, he fortified key places to secure what he had taken. Between 1066 and 1087 he set up 36 castles, among them Warwick Castle, which guarded against rebellion in the English Midlands.

paragraphs.heading: Changing designs
paragraphs.text: Many northern European castles began as earth and timber and had their defences rebuilt in stone later. Early ones often leaned on natural defences and a central keep, without towers. In the late 12th and early 13th centuries a more scientific approach took hold, and towers multiplied, with new weight placed on flanking fire. Many new castles were polygonal or concentric, with rings of defences one inside another that could all fight at once. These ideas blended techniques met on the Crusades with lessons from older works such as Roman forts.

paragraphs.heading: Show as well as strength
paragraphs.text: Not every feature was military. Moats, first dug for defence, turned into symbols of power, and some grand castles had long winding approaches meant to impress. A castle could serve as a stronghold and a prison, but also as a place where a lord entertained his equals. Over time looks mattered more, because a castle's size and appearance displayed the standing of the person living there, and comfortable homes were built inside the walls.

paragraphs.heading: Cannon and decline
paragraphs.text: Gunpowder reached Europe in the 14th century, but it changed castle building only in the 15th, once artillery could break stone walls. Castles were still built into the 16th century, yet the defences needed against stronger cannon made them uncomfortable places to live. True castles gave way to two separate things: artillery star forts with no part in civil government, and country houses that could not be defended.

paragraphs.heading: The word and its afterlife
paragraphs.text: The word castle comes from Latin castellum, a small form of castrum, 'fortified place'. It entered English shortly before the Norman Conquest of 1066, for a type of building then new to England. The name is sometimes used loosely for any fortification: Maiden Castle, for example, is really an Iron Age hill fort. From the 18th century, mock castles were built as part of a Gothic revival, with no military role at all.
